Use [cifreport()](#automated-reports) to generate a complete report from a dataset.
For tables from existing fits, see [Reporting cumulative incidence](#reporting-cumulative-incidence)
or [Reporting CIF regression](#reporting-cif-regression).

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
curve_ready <- requireNamespace("gtsummary", quietly = TRUE) &&
  utils::packageVersion("gtsummary") >= "2.6.1"
report_ready <- curve_ready && requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("rmarkdown", quietly = TRUE) && rmarkdown::pandoc_available()
regression_ready <- curve_ready && requireNamespace("broom.helpers", quietly = TRUE) &&
  utils::packageVersion("broom.helpers") >= "1.20.0"
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

## Automated survival and competing-risk reports {#automated-reports}

```{r setup-automated-reports, include=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = report_ready)
```

```{r dependencies-automated-reports, echo=FALSE, results='asis', eval=!report_ready}
cat("Install gtsummary, gt, knitr, and rmarkdown, and make Pandoc available to run the automated report example.")
```

`cifreport()` writes a Word, PDF, or self-contained HTML report and invisibly returns the
underlying tables, plots, fitted objects, and analysis log. Install
gtsummary (at least 2.6.1), gt, knitr, and rmarkdown, and make Pandoc
available to rmarkdown before running the example. Install xml2 and zip for
Word output.

### Two outcomes in one report

In the diabetes cohort, code 1 identifies diabetic retinopathy, code 2
identifies a macrovascular complication, and code 0 identifies censoring.
For the survival endpoint, either complication is an event. Both outcomes
use the same follow-up column in this example. An endpoint measured from
a different origin can name its own follow-up column.

Set `outcome.type = "survival"` or `"competing-risk"` for the report as a
whole, or set it in an individual outcome definition to override that choice.
With `NULL` or `"auto"`, each outcome is classified from the observed event
codes in the selected population before subgroup analysis. More than two
codes indicate competing risks. Specify `"competing-risk"` explicitly if
an expected event code is absent.

```{r report}
library(cifmodeling)
data(diabetes.complications)
cohort <- transform(diabetes.complications, all_event = epsilon != 0)

report <- cifreport(
  cohort,
  exposure = c("Fruit intake" = "fruitq1"),
  code.exposure.ref = 0,
  characteristics = c("age", "sex"),
  outcomes = list(
    Retinopathy = list(time = "t", event = "epsilon", time.point = c(4, 8)),
    "Complication-free survival" = list(
      time = "t", event = "all_event", outcome.type = "survival", time.point = c(3, 8)
    )
  ),
  overall = TRUE,
  filename.cifreport = tempfile(fileext = ".html")
)

report$tables$All[["Fruit intake"]]$table3
```

Omit `filename.cifreport` to write `yyyymmdd_cohort_analysis_report.docx` in the
current directory. To save to another directory, include that existing directory
in the filename, for example `filename.cifreport = "reports/cohort.html"`.
An existing file is overwritten after rendering. Use
`filename.cifreport = c("cohort.html", "cohort.docx", "cohort.pdf")` to save
all three formats from one analysis. Word tables are editable and use 9-point
text. By default, percentages in the tables use one decimal place. PDF output
requires Chrome, Chromium, or Microsoft Edge. Set `CIFREPORT_BROWSER` to
the executable path if the browser is not found automatically.
Set `filename.cifreport = NULL` to return the analysis without saving a file.
`report$output.file` returns the absolute paths in the order requested.
Set `data.name = "diabetes.complications"` to use the
original dataset name in the filename and the default report title.
Use `subset.condition = "age >= 50"` to restrict the analysis population.
Use `subgroup = "sex"` to report the selected population as a whole and each
observed level of `sex` within it. Use `exposure = c("Fruit intake" = "fruitq1", Sex = "sex")`
to add a grouping. Each population/exposure combination gets one section.
Factor levels determine group order. The first observed level is the default
risk-ratio reference. Use a named vector or list such as
`code.exposure.ref = list("Fruit intake" = 0)` to select references by exposure.

Use `level.strata = c(0, 1)`, `label.strata = c("Other intake", "Low intake")`,
and `order.strata = c(1, 0)` to display the low-intake group first in the
tables and curves. The reference is specified with its original code.
For multiple exposures, supply a named list for each strata argument,
such as `label.strata = list("Fruit intake" = c("0" = "Other intake", "1" = "Low intake"))`.
Subgroups use the same labels for their observed exposure levels.

Use `cifplot.args` to apply the same display settings to all figures,
including subgroup figures. For example, pass
`cifplot.args = list(label.x = "Years", breaks.x = c(0, 4, 8),
legend.position = "bottom", add.risktable = FALSE)` to `cifreport()`.
Use the report's strata arguments for exposure labels and display order,
which are shared by the tables and figures.

### Reading each section

1. **Patient characteristics.** A gtsummary table describes the subjects
   in each group. Missing baseline values appear in separate rows by
   default. Use `table1.args = list(label = list(age ~ "Age (years)"))`
   to change a label, or `overall = TRUE` to include the whole population.
   Characteristics with value labels (a named `labels` attribute) are
   summarized as categorical. Exposure value labels also appear in the table
   titles and are used as group labels unless overridden by `label.strata`.
   The p-value column compares the exposure groups using the default
   tests in `gtsummary::add_p()`. A characteristic needs at least two
   observed values and nonmissing data in at least two exposure groups to
   be tested.
   The text below the table gives group sizes and identifies characteristics
   with p-values below 0.05.
2. **Observed events over all follow-up.** The table names the time and event
   columns and shows primary, competing, and censoring counts alongside their codes.
   The text below it flags outcomes with fewer than five primary events in
   at least one exposure group.
3. **Cumulative counts and estimated probabilities.** Counts use
   `observed_time <= time.point` and include events tied at the requested
   time. Kaplan-Meier survival (KM) or primary-event Aalen-Johansen cumulative
   incidence (AJ) and pointwise confidence intervals use the same right-continuous
   convention. Enter times in the units of the follow-up column. Observed
   counts remain available beyond follow-up, where estimates and intervals
   are omitted for the affected groups. An outcome's `estimator` can request
   `"1-KM"` for event probability or `"1-AJ"` for the complement of the CIF.
   The text below the table gives the observed follow-up range across groups
   in the current analysis population and identifies nonpositive observed times.
4. **Crude risk ratios.** Each horizon has a separate intercept-only
   `polyreg()` nuisance model. For survival, the risk is one minus survival
   at the horizon. For competing risks, both cause-specific cumulative
   incidence ratios are reported from the joint fit. These are unadjusted
   associations. A requested horizon must be within the observed follow-up
   of every group, and a competing-risk fit requires both causes by that time.
5. **Curve comparison tests.** The log-rank test compares survival curves
   and Gray's test compares primary-event cumulative incidence curves over
   follow-up. Each outcome has one test per section.

Each outcome with an available fit gets its own numbered figure. By default
the figure uses the same estimator scale as Table 3 and shows the group
labels and risk table. `cifplot.args = list(type.y = "cumhaz")` changes the
figure scale while Table 3 keeps the selected estimator.

### Supported data and analysis status

The report supports unweighted right-censored follow-up with one row per
subject, distinct non-negative integer codes, and one competing code per
competing-risk outcome. Logical events and numeric codes stored as factor
levels or character strings are supported. Supported comparisons include
binary and multi-level groups. Left truncation, time-dependent covariates,
recurrent events, adjustment, and simultaneous confidence bands are
outside the reporting interface.

Rows where a subset condition evaluates to `NA` are excluded. Within each
subset, missing group values skip the section. Missing follow-up
times or event values skip the affected outcome. An empty population
produces a status entry. With a single observed group, the report keeps
the descriptive tables and plot. An absent reference level affects risk
ratios only. The status log records these cases as well as unsupported
horizons, warnings and estimation failures. A failure in one fit leaves
unrelated results available.

Subjects with missing subgroup values contribute to the overall analysis.
For a subgroup level with zero observed events for an outcome, the report
includes the counts in Table 2 and skips Tables 3–5 and Figure 1 for that
outcome. In a competing-risk outcome, either a primary event or a competing
event counts toward this check.

## Reporting cumulative incidence {#reporting-cumulative-incidence}

```{r setup-reporting-cumulative-incidence, include=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = curve_ready)
```

```{r dependencies-reporting-cumulative-incidence, echo=FALSE, results='asis', eval=!curve_ready}
cat("Install gtsummary version 2.6.1 or later to run these cumulative incidence examples.")
```

### A cumulative incidence table

The examples use a reproducible sample of 200 records from the anonymized
`diabetes.complications` cohort. Follow-up is measured in years; event 1 is
diabetic retinopathy and event 2 is a macrovascular complication. The estimates
illustrate how to report retinopathy probabilities by fruit-intake group.

```{r first-table}
library(cifmodeling)
library(gtsummary)
data(diabetes.complications)
set.seed(1)
report_data <- diabetes.complications[
  sample.int(nrow(diabetes.complications), 200L), ]
report_data$fruitq1 <- factor(report_data$fruitq1, levels = c(0, 1),
                            labels = c("Other intake", "Low intake"))

curve <- cifcurve(Event(t, epsilon) ~ fruitq1, data = report_data,
                  outcome.type = "competing-risk")
cif_table <- tbl_survfit(curve, times = c(4, 8), type = "risk",
                         label_header = "**{time}-year CIF**")
cif_table
```

For competing risks, the `survfit`-compatible object stores `surv = 1 - CIF`.
The `type = "risk"` argument displays the CIF and reverses the saved interval
limits: the reported limits are `1 - upper` and `1 - lower`. The table does
not re-fit the curve or construct a different confidence interval.

### Selecting confidence intervals

Choose inference when fitting the curve. Here IF-based standard errors,
Student critical values and a log-log transformation are requested. For the
stored `1 - CIF`, this transformation is the complementary log-log
transformation of the CIF.

```{r student-intervals}
student_curve <- cifcurve(Event(t, epsilon) ~ fruitq1, data = report_data,
  outcome.type = "competing-risk", error = "if", conf.dist = "t",
  conf.type = "log-log")
student_table <- tbl_survfit(student_curve, times = c(4, 8), type = "risk",
  label_header = "**{time}-year CIF**") |>
  modify_footnote_header(columns = all_stat_cols(),
    footnote = "95% pointwise IF-t intervals; log-log transformation of 1 - CIF; deletion allocation for degrees of freedom.")
student_table
```

`error = "fay"` selects the Fay--Graubard-type variance correction, and
`df.method = "equal"` is an alternative allocation for IF-t. Supplied weights
are treated as fixed. Details of the inference methods are in `?cifcurve`.
Degrees of freedom vary by group and time; they are available in a summary
without adding diagnostic columns to the publication table.

```{r inference-diagnostics}
s <- summary(student_curve, times = c(4, 8), extend = TRUE)
data.frame(group = s$strata, time = s$time, df = s$df,
           interval_status = s$conf.status)
```

An unavailable interval remains missing. In particular, a valid interval is
not carried beyond the last positive-weight follow-up. Exact structural
boundaries retain the fitted singleton interval. These are pointwise
intervals, not simultaneous confidence bands.

### Comparing curves through a specified horizon

The following tests compare the CIF curves through 8 years. They are not
separate tests of the probabilities in each column of the preceding table.
The score tests emphasize earlier or later differences through their
Fleming--Harrington weights. The method labels are taken from the saved fits.

```{r curve-tests}
tests <- list(
  gray = ciftest(Event(t, epsilon) ~ fruitq1, report_data,
                 test = "gray", tau = 8),
  early = ciftest(Event(t, epsilon) ~ fruitq1, report_data,
                  test = "score", rho = 1, gamma = 0, tau = 8),
  late = ciftest(Event(t, epsilon) ~ fruitq1, report_data,
                 test = "score", rho = 0, gamma = 1, tau = 8)
)
test_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tests, function(fit) {
  x <- generics::tidy(fit)
  data.frame(method = paste(x$method, x$weight), p.value = x$p.value)
}))
test_table <- as_gtsummary(test_results) |>
  modify_header(method = "**Curve comparison through 8 years**",
                p.value = "**p-value**") |>
  modify_fmt_fun(p.value = label_style_pvalue(digits = 3))
test_table
```

This recipe reports the selected `ciftest()` results directly. The usual
`add_p()` default for a survival table is a log-rank test and does not select
these CIF tests. The ordinary Gray branch supports integer frequency
weights; it does not treat fractional IPTW as frequency weights.

To include the statistic and degrees of freedom, select `statistic` and
`parameter` from `generics::tidy(fit)`. The latter is the effective rank of
the test covariance, distinct from the time-specific Student degrees of
freedom used for the curve intervals.

### Labels and risk-set counts

Use gtsummary's existing label, header and formatting arguments to customize
the table. For a weighted fit, distinguish the number of observations,
the sum of weights and the effective sample size. `n.risk.type` chooses the
quantity exposed as `n.risk`; the legacy `n.risk`, `n.event` and `n.censor`
fields are rounded upward, while `n.risk.weighted`, `n.risk.unweighted` and
`n.risk.ess` retain their respective values on the native grid. An event count
in this curve object includes both event causes, not only retinopathy.

### Exporting the table

The table can be converted with standard gtsummary methods. The temporary
paths below can be replaced with the desired output filenames.

```{r export-cif}
html_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".html")
gt::gtsave(as_gt(student_table), filename = html_file)
```

```{r export-cif-word, eval=curve_ready && requireNamespace('flextable', quietly=TRUE)}
word_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".docx")
flextable::save_as_docx(as_flex_table(student_table), path = word_file)
```

## Reporting CIF regression {#reporting-cif-regression}

```{r setup-reporting-cif-regression, include=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = regression_ready)
```

```{r dependencies-reporting-cif-regression, echo=FALSE, results='asis', eval=!regression_ready}
cat("Install gtsummary version 2.6.1 or later and broom.helpers version 1.20.0 or later to run these regression examples.")
```

### An event-specific regression table

Fit the direct CIF regression, then pass the result to `tbl_regression()`.
The example uses the anonymized diabetes cohort from the overview. Effects
compare low fruit intake with the reference group at 8 years; age and sex
enter the nuisance model. See the direct regression vignette for model
assumptions and estimation details.

```{r first-regression-table}
library(cifmodeling)
library(gtsummary)
data(diabetes.complications)
report_data <- diabetes.complications
report_data$fruitq1 <- factor(report_data$fruitq1, levels = c(0, 1),
                            labels = c("Other intake", "Low intake"))
attr(report_data$fruitq1, "label") <- "Fruit intake"
fit <- polyreg(Event(t, epsilon) ~ age + sex, exposure = "fruitq1",
  code.exposure.ref = "Other intake", data = report_data, time.point = 8,
  effect.measure1 = "RR", effect.measure2 = "RR")

retinopathy_table <- tbl_regression(fit, exponentiate = TRUE)
retinopathy_table
```

The default event is event 1, diabetic retinopathy. The table reports
exponentiated effect estimates and their saved confidence limits. Standard
errors and test statistics remain on the coefficient's log scale. The
reference row describes the contrast; it is not an additional estimated
coefficient. These observational estimates do not by themselves establish
a causal effect of fruit intake.

### Reporting the competing event

Select event 2 explicitly to report macrovascular complications. The
numeric results, exposure labels and effect-measure heading all follow
the selected event.

```{r competing-event}
macrovascular_table <- tbl_regression(fit, exponentiate = TRUE, event = "event2")
tbl_merge(list(retinopathy_table, macrovascular_table),
  tab_spanner = c("**Retinopathy**", "**Macrovascular complications**"))
```

For a tidy data frame containing both events, use
`generics::tidy(fit, event = "both")`. Publication regression tables select
one event at a time and are combined with `tbl_merge()`.

### RR, OR and SHR

Choose the effect measure during estimation, not while formatting the table.
RR compares cumulative incidence probabilities, OR compares their odds, and
SHR is the subdistribution hazard ratio parameterization. At a fixed time,
the latter is the ratio of `-log(1 - CIF)` values; it is not a cause-specific
hazard ratio. Run the following code interactively to compare the three models
for the same exposure and 8-year target.

```{r effect-measures, eval=FALSE}
fit_or <- polyreg(Event(t, epsilon) ~ age + sex, exposure = "fruitq1",
  code.exposure.ref = "Other intake", data = report_data, time.point = 8,
  effect.measure1 = "OR", effect.measure2 = "OR")
fit_shr <- polyreg(Event(t, epsilon) ~ age + sex, exposure = "fruitq1",
  code.exposure.ref = "Other intake", data = report_data, time.point = 8,
  effect.measure1 = "SHR", effect.measure2 = "SHR")
tbl_merge(list(tbl_regression(fit, exponentiate = TRUE),
               tbl_regression(fit_or, exponentiate = TRUE),
               tbl_regression(fit_shr, exponentiate = TRUE)),
  tab_spanner = c("**RR model**", "**OR model**", "**SHR model**"))
```

The two events can also use different effect measures. Headings are read
from the fitted `estimand` information; no effect measure is inferred from
the size of a coefficient.

```{r mixed-effect-measures}
fit_mixed <- polyreg(Event(t, epsilon) ~ age + sex, exposure = "fruitq1",
  code.exposure.ref = "Other intake", data = report_data, time.point = 8,
  effect.measure1 = "RR", effect.measure2 = "SHR")
tbl_merge(list(tbl_regression(fit_mixed, exponentiate = TRUE),
               tbl_regression(fit_mixed, exponentiate = TRUE, event = "event2")),
  tab_spanner = c("**Retinopathy**", "**Macrovascular complications**"))
```

### Confidence intervals and labels

With unchanged inference settings, the table extracts the fitted intervals.
This also applies to stored bootstrap intervals: they are not replaced by
Wald limits during exponentiation. To retain the fitted confidence level
explicitly, pass `conf.level = fit$conf.int`. A request for a different level
uses the existing supported reconstruction, or fails if the saved method
cannot provide that level without refitting, as with BCa limits.

```{r labels}
tbl_regression(fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.level = fit$conf.int,
               label = list(fruitq1 ~ "Low fruit intake versus other intake"))
```

For direct extraction, `generics::tidy(fit)` retains log-scale estimates.
Use `exponentiate = TRUE` for ratios. The broom convention uses logical
`conf.int` and numeric `conf.level`; the older numeric `conf.int` argument
remains accepted by `tidy.polyreg()` for compatibility. There is no need to
modify the saved fit or supply a custom tidier to produce these tables.

### Exporting a regression table

`polyreg()` retains the exposure's variable and value labels for reporting.
Use `label.exposure` to override the variable label and a named
`label.strata` vector to override selected exposure levels. The names of
that vector are the original exposure codes.

`modelsummary::msummary(as_modelsummary(fit, event = "event1"))` uses the
stored display labels after the fit is saved and restored. `coef(fit)`,
`tidy(fit)`, and direct `msummary(fit)` keep the original coefficient keys.
Set `display.labels = FALSE` in `as_modelsummary()` to keep those keys in
its output for `coef_map` or `coef_omit`.

Use the standard gtsummary conversions. Replace the temporary filenames
with the intended destination when saving the final report.

```{r export-regression}
html_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".html")
gt::gtsave(as_gt(retinopathy_table), filename = html_file)
```

```{r export-regression-word, eval=regression_ready && requireNamespace('flextable', quietly=TRUE)}
word_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".docx")
flextable::save_as_docx(as_flex_table(retinopathy_table), path = word_file)
```
